articles.text: At the earliest start of school in Piedmont history, students and parents shifted gears on Tuesday, August 8, with walkthrough registration at Piedmont Middle and High Schools. Students at both campuses were given their class schedules for the year. The ambiance could not have been more different. At 1:30 p.m. on Tuesday, the middle school’s walkthrough registration in the Buzz Redford Gym was jam packed. In contrast, in Sukanya Goswami’s second year as principal of Piedmont High School, parent volunteers and high school clubs were well spaced out on the campus. Walkthrough registration is more than just getting your planner and finding out if you got your desired electives. It is also a day for students to see long lost friends after the summer break and to rekindle the back-to-school excitement. Middle schoolers, many of whom were accompanied by parents or guardians, shuffled in line for photos in the gym, then headed to the library to pick up their schedules. Last year, middle school registration was spread out more, with photos being taken in the John Morrison Gym. Long lines didn’t seem to concern students though as they happily socialized inside and on the patio.

articles.text: As the project to replace turf and irrigation at Witter Field continues, neighbors are increasingly concerned about flooding impacts. In 2007, when new synthetic turf was last installed at Witter, it cost $219,000 and was installed in two weeks by FieldTurf, the company manufacturing the product of the same name. When the current project began on June 6, 2023, the turf was eight years past its eight-year life span. Since then, the field has often flooded and been unplayable for sports due to an apparent insufficient drainage system. The project now has a $4,150,000 price tag and a sixmonth project span. The proposed new irrigation system involves rerouting a storm drain from its current location under the field, to a Bushy Dell Creek manhole. However, some neighbors on Palm Drive, by the base of the field, raise questions not yet sufficiently answered by the Piedmont Unified School District. They maintain that the district, responsible for overseeing the renovation, has not adequately studied flood risks that this project may present to their homes. articles.text: At a public hearing on Monday, August 14, at 5:30 p.m., the Planning Commission will consider two proposals to make new housing easier to build in Piedmont: pre-approved design plans for affordable ADUs and objective design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings. If the Commission approves the proposals, they will advance to the City Council for adoption. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). This proposal would allow Piedmont property owners who submit these preapproved designs as-is to receive a planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the development process. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. However, the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Multifamily objective design standards (MODS) Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The MODS don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. generally urban infill areas, which comprise less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Community members can submit comments on the proposals ahead of the meeting by email to PiedmontIsHome@piedmont. ca.gov; by mail to the Piedmont Planning Commission, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or speak on the topic at the 5:30 p.m. August 14 meeting in-person or via Zoom. The agenda report for both items is available for download on PiedmontIsHome.org. articles.text: Fire Dept. asks residents to eliminate fire hazards As summer heat continues and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. Recent wildfires across California have taught us that our communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said that homeowners’ responsibility for fire prevention “is whatever is on your property. Cities take care of the trees and vegetation in the public rights-of-way and the parks.” “Ideally,” he said, “people should leave at least five feet of room between vegetation and flammable property (like homes, fences and decks), and 10 feet between tree limbs and roofs or chimneys.” To prevent ladder fuel – a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the ground upward to tree or shrub canopies – Brannigan said “for the height of the fuel, you want three times the amount of space above it, so if you have one foot of grass, try to have three feet between whatever is above it.” Although property owners may find their yards in particularly dangerous situations this fire season due to high vegetation growth after last winter’s rainstorms, Brannigan said “We have a saying that every year is going to be the worst fire season, whether its dry and drought or whether it’s wet and a lot of growth.” He urged Piedmonters to clear their yards of dead and excess vegetation as soon as possible, ahead of the dryer months of September and October. In Piedmont particularly, he said, “We have a lot of beautiful old homes; some have wood siding and wood shingles. Having vegetation right up against that or overhanging with debris falling down” presents a particular danger in lieu of regular tree and shrub maintenance. In the Bay Area more broadly, he continued, “when you look at statewide [fire] guidance, it often involves five feet, thirty feet, a hundred feet, but we just don’t have that kind of space. We are trying to come up with practical, realistic guidelines to keep your property safe as well as the adjacent properties and prevent fire from spreading.” Just as crucial is the knowledge of evacuation routes, “Know, from where you live, work, go to school, at least two ways out of your neighborhood, Also know multiple ways you can get yourself out, whether by car, by walking, whether you’re in a wheelchair or on a bicycle. Talk with your neighbors and find out if there are people around you who might need a little bit of extra help.” In short: to increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire, create space between plants and your home, and clear your yard of any debris or flammable materials like dead vegetation. If you need help with firesafe landscaping or with identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 to request an inspection. If you’d like to get a head start on preparing your household, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ wildfire and piedmont.ca.gov/ vegetation for more recommendations on preparing your household. A checklist for preparing your yard is available at piedmont.ca.gov/YardChecklist.

articles.text: Kerry Persichitte has been selected to lead PCC’s new NextGen ministry program. Piedmont Community Church will host a community picnic in Piedmont Park on Sunday, August 20, at 11 a.m. The event will have food, live music and children’s games as part of the church’s celebration of a new youth ministry, NextGen. Kerry Persichitte, who has been hired to lead the program, said the church is starting the new ministry “to find out how we can best serve kids — from the ages of three months all the way through 18 — so they can build their faith, develop fun relationships with friends, and feel supported by their parents. I’m excited for the picnic on the 20th, when NextGen officially launches, to reflect that combination of safety, community, faith, fun, and a sense of belonging.” The ministry will involve age-divided groups - including a nursery, a pre-kindergarten program, and respective programs for elementary, middle school and high school students. “Worship will involve largegroup communicators that really bring the Bible stories to life, and what we call ‘life groups,’ which will be smaller spaces to give the kids a chance to discuss or share whatever they’d like, with a trusted adult or fellow student,” Persichitte said. A veteran of 17 years developing youth ministry in churches across the country, from Illinois to New jersey to California, has affirmed the importance of student leadership and parent collaboration in helping shape worship programs. “Kids today want to have a lot of agency in their environments and know best what’s going on in their worlds,” she continued. “With NextGen, we’ll always be asking the kids involved: ‘What is it you need?’ We want them to help create a space they’re proud of, feel safe in, and that they want to invite their friends to.” On Sunday, Aug. 20, at 11 a.m., Piedmont Community Church will hold a family picnic in Piedmont Park celebrating the launch of its new NextGen youth ministry program, directed by Kerry Persichitte (above). Furthermore, she added, “Despite how overconnected we all are with social media, I think there’s an overwhelming sense of loneliness in our culture. Staying culturally relevant is an issue that is important for anyone who wants to create that sense of belonging. We’ll focus on bringing the Bible to life for these kids in relevant ways that can impact their everyday lives, and developing safe relationships where they can share struggles they’re facing in their lives. A key part of that, too, will involve partnering with parents, and offering support to them in dealing with these struggles that kids face, like anxiety and the place of social media.” “The heart of what we want kids and parents to take from NextGen,” she concluded, “is a sense of purpose and connection. We want kids to know that we believe in their future. They are the world changers, they are the future of this world, and we want to do everything that we can to support them through the church.” For more information visit PiedmontChurch.org or call the church at 547-5700. articles.text: Vegetation management plays a critical role in reducing wildfire risk to our community. It is important to take time every year to prune plants and clear debris before fire season. Use this checklist to prepare your property in early summer, then review it again in September. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! articles.text: Highlander Robotics, an FRC team in the FIRST Robotics program, is hosting an Open House at Piedmont High School on Friday, August 11, at 6 pm. The team encourages interested 9th to 12th grade students and their parents to learn more about the team and this season’s robot “Paddo the Frog,” who just returned from the Houston World Championships. The event will include a presentation of the program as well as a demo of the robot. Working under the mentorship of experienced industry professionals, members are guided through the build process with full support. Team members gain real-world engineering experience and get to work in a constructive learning environment amongst other like-minded and passionate team members. When prompted with a fieldgame challenge at the start of each build season, student members get an opportunity to learn and apply the fabrication, design, prototyping and coding skills learned during the off-season training that takes place each fall. Highlander Robotics welcomes all students regardless of experience. “Our program expects to train students from scratch. We believe that anyone can become a leader on the team if they have the interest and can dedicate the time,” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark. The Highlanders provide training in programming, CAD (computer aided design), and general mechanical work. Outside of more traditional robotics work, Highlander Robotics also seeks members with other diverse interests including community outreach, visual and industrial design, marketing, branding, video production and other roles needed to display a well-functioning robotics team. To learn more, come meet the team this week, August 11, in the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab in the STEAM Building. For more information, visit frc8033.com, or contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.org. Piedmont’s Highlander Robotics team at the World Championships in Houston, Texas.

articles.text: PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy and Information in Special Education) announced this week that it has changed its name to PIE (Piedmonters for Inclusive Education). Why change our name? We believe that Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) best reflects who we are at this time in our organizational history,” said board president Iris Warchall. We are parents who support inclusion in PUSD for all students with disabilities and learning differences. We believe that all learners have the right to full participation and inclusion in our classrooms and in our community, and that for us to do so as a community we must work to meet the needs of students with all neurotypes, abilities, and learning styles. We strive to ensure that the Piedmont Unified School District provides all students with an excellent education in a nurturing environment. “We will continue to advocate for resources to help meet students’ access needs, provide educational resources in the form of our well-loved Neurodiversity Speaker Series and provide grants to PUSD teachers and Piedmont Recreation Department programs that help make Piedmont a welcoming community for all,” added Warchall.

articles.text: The oldest rowing club in the East Bay is launching a new rowing program for competitive high schoolers. Lake Merritt Rowing Club, founded in 1962, is starting a team that will be capped in size and will focus on individualized coaching for aspiring high school rowers. Lake Merritt’s competitive program is geared to accommodate young athletes who want to compete at a high level without sacrificing on family, academic and other obligations. Lake Merritt Rowing Club has its boathouse in the Lake Chalet building directly on Lake Merritt. Although the club has trained recreational youth rowers for decades, this is its initial foray into youth competitive teams. Rick Gallagher, a Piedmont resident and President of the Club, explained the motivation behind the new program. “We have amazing coaches and a boathouse in one of the best spots in the Bay Area. We have all the ingredients for a top high school program. We felt that the community needed a program for kids who want to row fast, but who also need a more flexible approach given family and academic pressures.” The head coach for Lake Merritt’s competitive youth team will be Heather Krakora, a former Division I rower for the University of Minnesota who is still a top rower in the adult competitive ranks. “My own rowing journey began on a small, tight-knit squad. I was forever shaped by my rowing team that was like family – together we pushed one another to be our best while building strong bonds,” said Krakora. “That unforgettable experience sparked a lifelong love of rowing that I can’t wait to instill in Lake Merritt’s Competitive Youth team.” In addition to offering a small team environment, Lake Merritt’s program will offer more scheduling flexibility for high school rowers who also need to focus on academics, family and other sports. The key to flexibility is its Heather Krakora recently was named head coach of Lake Merritt Rowing Club’s new youth competitive crew. small team and a focus on smaller boats. “We’re focused on creating an environment where driven young athletes can thrive on their own terms,” said Krakora. “By keeping the team small and flexible, we empower each rower to balance the sport with the other important parts of their lives.” Lake Merritt is limiting its team to only 16 participants. This is a departure from the traditional approach, in which young athletes are separated into larger boats and ranked. “On a small team, each athlete’s individual progress helps motivate the entire crew.” Krakora added, “There’s a special sense of trust and friendship that develops when a group is focused, driven, and working toward the same goals.” Lake Merritt’s boathouse is located directly under the Lake Chalet restaurant. It docks in the historic 100-year-old pump house renovated by the City of Oakland in 2004. Gallagher noted that Lake Merritt’s rowers get the benefit of some of the safest and flattest water in the Bay Area. “Rowing out in the Bay can be rough with all the wind and boats moving around. We’re lucky that the only obstacle in the Lake comes from ducks from the bird preserve.” Lake Merritt’s team, once filled, will start practices in September and will compete in regattas this Fall and Spring. Practices will run Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from 4:15 pm to 6:30 pm and on Saturdays from 9:30am to noon. One practice per week will be on land and focused on strength and fitness. Athletes will be permitted to choose whether to participate in weekend regattas based on their individual academic and other commitments and their desire to compete in events. Registration is now open on Lake Merritt Rowing Club’s website and will remain open until 16 team member slots are filled. Interested families may contact the Club’s President (Rick Gallagher) or Youth Competitive Coach (Heather Krakora) by emailing President@LakeMerrittRowingClub.org or CoachHeather@LakeMerrittRowingClub.org.

articles.text: The fall of 2023 marks a first for many high schools in California to introduce girls’ flag football to go from being a club sport to official status. Entering its inaugural season as an official Piedmont High sport is the Highlanders’ girls’ flag football team, currently training at Humphries Diamond’s ahead of Week 1 in September. “I see a lot of girls who are hungry to play football and are so excited to be out here. We are making sure it’s real football. They have more skills than we expected, we’ve been impressed from Day 1. I like their hustle, their mindset, and they’re smart. We have intelligent girls, I think that will make a big difference for us,” said head coach Beth Black, who in her spare time moonlights as the head of the school’s English Department. Piedmont will be a part of an 8-team league competing in the Western Alameda County Conference with Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, Hayward, San Leandro, and Tennyson. The season opens with a League Jamboree featuring all eight schools on Saturday, September 9 at Mt. Eden (Hayward) , followed by Piedmont playing a seven-game schedule before the WACC’s Championship Tournament on October 28 at Hayward High. No Section playoffs are being offered in its first year of competition. For PHS student athletes takStaff Photos Friedie Schickedanz throws a pass in Piedmont’s girls’ flag football practice ahead of its inaugural season. ing part in the team, it marks an exciting time as the players help build a program from its ground-level. They’ll represent the trend-setters for a completely new sport, being a major part of creating traditions like the other established sports at the school. “This is the first year, where no one has really played as a team, so we’re all learning together. We’re sort of like the guinea pigs, we’re setting the trend,” said Dahlia Osman. Day 1 of its season started this week on Monday, August 7. With Witter Field unusable to a major renovation project, the team is practicing on Humphries Diamond, the baseball field. Students Head coach Beth Black directs defensive drills at a practice. Mia Leggett gets ready to receive a long pass during offensive drills. took part in flag-pulling drills, running routes, and worked on their defensive and offensive formations. Piedmont is still in the phase of determining who plays what positions and hammering home the fundamentals of the game. “I really don’t know a lot about football, but I came in excited. I play soccer, but I wanted to try something new. I’ve always just watched football, like on TV or at the high school games, so it’s really interesting to learn the positions and nuances of the game,” said Elspeth Grippando. It’s difficult to say who is emerging as leaders, but making their presence felt were multisport athletes such as Friedie Schickedanz (water polo and lacrosse), Ella Yasar (track), Juliana Thornborrow (soccer), and Mia Leggett from the softball team. Leggett has been a member of the softball team and was on the varsity basketball team in 2022. At Monday’s practice, Leggett was proving herself as a playmaker with sure-hands, agility, and an understanding of route-running, making a clean over-the-shoulder catch on a fade route. She credits her knowledge of football to her time throwing the ball around the yard with her father and being in a family of devout Raiders fans. Leggett, a senior at PHS, now has an opportunity to play the game she loves in an organized league. “Football has always been a part of my life. I played softball and basketball, some of the same mechanics apply here, like with route-running, so it’s kind of been easier to adjust in practice. My family has been Raiders fans through thick and thin, they still are. I grew up with the game, just throwing the football with my dad. Sports have always been a big part of my life,” said Leggett. Piedmont’s current schedule isn’t yet official. A s it stands, following the season-opening jamboree on September 9, Piedmont will play games at Alameda on September 15, Mt. Eden on September 22, Encinal on September 28, and host its first flag football game on October 5 versus Berkeley.

articles.text: After waking up early Sunday morning, I kept rubbing my eyes to grasp the reality of seeing the U.S. Women’s Soccer Team, the two-time World Cup champion, losing in the Round of 16 to Sweden 5-4 in penalty kicks after ending regulation and overtime in a 0-0 deadlock. USWNT supporters likely experienced all the stages of grief: denial, anger, depression, and a harsh dose of reality. Much like their earlier three matches in the Group stage, the United States just couldn’t find the finishing touch despite having its chances. They outshot the Swedes 22 to nine, including 11 shots on target to Sweden’s one. Sweden’s goalkeeper Zecira Musovic was amazing, standing on her head to make 11 saves with five by dives, stopping nine shots from inside the box. Each stop by Musovic seemed to take the life out of the United States, which were uncharacteristically inconsistent on open situations. The nerves perhaps carried into penalty kicks. The U.S. was up 3-2 after Nathalie Björn skied a shot for Sweden. However, what followed was unimaginable. Megan Rapinoe, Sophie Smith, and Kelley O’Hara, three of the team’s best goal scorers all went wide-right, allowing Sweden to march back to a 4-4 deadlock and just needing to convert the winner. It couldn’t have been more dramatic with Lina Hurtig’s shot initially stopped by U.S. goalkeeper Alyssa Naeher, only for it to loop in the air and cross the goal line for the winning goal. It was a result many soccer fans felt was coming after the United States finished second in the 3-team Group E. Photo courtesy of NBC Sports The United States took its earliest exit from the World Cup in team history after falling 5-4 to Sweden in penalty kicks. Japan will face Sweden in the Quarterfinals and are the favorites despite having a lower world ranking. England is the current favorite to win the entire World Cup. They were the recent UEFA 2022 European Champion but are without their lead player. Photo courtesy of AP News Sweden celebrates after defeating the United States in penalty kicks. Hinata Miyazawa of Japan is the Golden Boot leader with five goals, while Mina Tanaka has been instrumental with three assists and two goals. It’s hard to pick against Japan, so I’m going with a 2-1 win for the Japanese. No. 4 England vs. No. 25 Colombia England is currently favored to win the entire World Cup which is somewhat surprising after going to penalty kicks against Nigeria, winning 4-2 after ending overtime in a 0-0 tie. Key player, Lauren James, was red carded and will miss the quarterfinals against Colombia. But England gets their favored status after winning the 2022 European Women’s Championship, so their praise despite losing James and barely getting by Nigeria is well-deserved. They should still get the job done against lowly ranked Colombia. I’m not going with an upset, 2-0 Three Lions of England. No. 5 France vs. No. 10 Australia The French are coming in on a strong run of form after defeating No. 72 Morocco and winning a difficult Group F over Jamaica and Brazil, but Australia, the host country will have a large rooting section. . France boasts Kadidiatou Diani, who has four goals and three assists thus far. I’m going France 3-1. No. 6 Spain vs. No. 9 Netherlands Spain is another favorite to win it all by beating the Netherlands. The Spaniards demolished Switzerland in the Round of 16, while the Dutch had a strong 2-0 win over South Africa. The Netherlands won Group E over the United States and are led by Jill Roord, who has four goals thus far.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre in San Francisco premieres Hippest Trip – The Soul Train Musical on August 25. Soul Train is based on the iconic TV show that originally aired on Chicago airwaves in the 1970’s. For over 30 years, it brought Black music, dance, and style into living rooms in America and was a celebration of black youth culture. The show’s self-proclaimed reputation was “the hippest trip in America,” hence the musical’s title. The creative team behind ACT’s reimagined Soul Train includes Tony Award–nominated playwright Dominique Morisseau known for The Detroit Project, Tony Award–nominated choreographer Camille A. Brown, and Apollo Theater’s executive director Kamilah Forbes. Playwright Morisseau said she is looking forward to partnering with an all-female creative team to celebrate “the history and unsung heroes of our nation’s longest running televised music and dance series.” ACT’s Hippest Trip - The Soul Train Musical “I am so excited to help bring the narrative of one of our culture’s most influential and legend-making endeavors to the stage. Having grown up on this series and being immersed in the culture around it, I never knew what it took to make it the iconic staple that it is,” she said. The cast includes Angela Birchett as Delores, Quentin Earl Darrington as Don Cornelius, Amber Iman as Pam Brown, and Kayla Davion as Jody Watley. articles.text: The 19th annual Sculpture in the Garden at Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek ends this Sunday, August 13. Sculpture in the Garden is the annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural art with the natural beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features art installations and sculptures by local craftsmen. The event also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available for purchase. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is now exhibiting Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. The exhibit will be on view through September 10. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ SF MOMA’s exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “The exhibition offers an oppor tunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded,” said Christopher Bedford, Art Director at SF MOMA. “This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org.

articles.text: To call Quentin Tarantino’s film, Inglourious Basterds, a solid B-movie may seem a bit cranky. After all, it does have its A-movie moments. The opening of the film demonstrates Tarantino’s unassailable talent as a writer-director. It’s a set piece in which a German SS Colonel., Hans Landa (Christop Waltz), arrives at a French dairy farm to interview the farmer. The year is 1941 and the words, “Once upon a time in Nazi-occupied France…” flash on the screen. Landa, known as Hitler’s Jew Hunter, arrives at the farm because he suspects the farmer is hiding a Jewish family. The scene, wonderfully framed inside the farmhouse, is filled with menace, even more chilling because of Landa’s exaggerated civility and calm. In that moment, the Col. is a distillation of the evil perpetrated by the Nazis as they set about finding and then exterminating a people. As Landa slowly drinks a cold glass of milk, while discoursing on Jews as rats, the camera pans to the cracks in the floorboards. It’s quickly apparent that a family is lying just below, listening and watching, hands held over their mouths, as the moment unfolds. They are clearly terrified. This scene and its outcome could easily be a remarkable, stand alone short possessing an intense arc and a perfect, if unexpected, denouement. But because the film is divided into chapters, a new scene quickly begins which introduces the inglourious Basterds, a small group of American Jewish G.I.s, led by Lt. Aldo Raines (Brad Pitt), a Tennessee good old boy who wants not only to kill Nazis but take their scalps as well. Pitt’s over the top portrayal approaches caricature and the film flirts with farce. It’s a surprising decision by Tarantino, for this group of behind the lines commandos (OSS) should be quietly lethal and profoundly serious about what’s a stake, not simply a congregation of idiosyncratic psychopaths unleashed on the Third Reich. It soon becomes evident that the hunt for Jews by Col. Landa will not be the contextual backdrop of the film, but merely an isolated vignette. And so the film abruptly jumps to 1944, the story now focused on Shoshana Dreyfus (Melanie Laurent), owner of a small Paris cinema (inherited from her aunt and uncle), and pursued romantically by a German war hero, Frederick Zoller (Daniel Bruhl). The film then cuts to the second nicely constructed scene that takes place in a Parisian bistro, involving British and American soldiers dressed in Nazi uniforms, their mission being to contact German movie star Bridget von Hammersmark (Diane Kruger), a British undercover agent. Like the opening, this set piece is fraught with tension, is wonderfully shot, and even with its concluding Mexican standoff represents Tarantino at his best. But where the film falls away is in its inability to tell a fully coherent story with compelling characters that connect with each other and with the audience. Ultimately, despite the vignettes, or because of the disparate vignettes, there is no there there; the film has no sustaining center. Tarantino can almost blithely skirt the horror of the extermination of the Jews, perpetrated by monsters like Landa, and turn Landa, decked out in his tailored SS uniform and gleaming black riding boots, into the most attractive and authentic hustler in the film. This is not a film about distilled evil but about scenarios leading to a blazing climax where revisionist history takes place inside a burning cinema in Paris. If Schindler’s List is the yin, then Inglourious Basterds is the yang. Regarding the unusual spelling of the film’s title – Inglourious Basterds – apparently it’s an obscure reference to an Italian knock-off film of The Dirty Dozen, reflecting nothing more than Tarantino’s quirky style and no more. It’s a set piece in which a German SS Colonel., Hans Landa (Christop Waltz), arrives at a French dairy farm to interview the farmer. The year is 1941 and the words, “Once upon a time in Nazi-occupied France…” flash on the screen. Landa, known as Hitler’s Jew Hunter, arrives at the farm because he suspects the farmer is hiding a Jewish family. The scene, wonderfully framed inside the farmhouse, is filled with menace, even more chilling because of Landa’s exaggerated civility and calm. In that moment, the Col. is a distillation of the evil perpetrated by the Nazis as they set about finding and then exterminating a people. As Landa slowly drinks a cold glass of milk, while discoursing on Jews as rats, the camera pans to the cracks in the floorboards. It’s quickly apparent that a family is lying just below, listening and watching, hands held over their mouths, as the moment unfolds. They are clearly terrified. This scene and its outcome could easily be a remarkable, stand alone short possessing an intense arc and a perfect, if unexpected, denouement. But because the film is divided into chapters, a new scene quickly begins which introduces the inglourious Basterds, a small group of American Jewish G.I.s, led by Lt. Aldo Raines (Brad Pitt), a Tennessee good old boy who wants not only to kill Nazis but take their scalps as well. Pitt’s over the top portrayal approaches caricature and the film flirts with farce. It’s a surprising decision by Tarantino, for this group of behind the lines commandos (OSS) should be quietly lethal and profoundly serious about what’s a stake, not simply a congregation of idiosyncratic psychopaths unleashed on the Third Reich. It soon becomes evident that the hunt for Jews by Col. Landa will not be the contextual backdrop of the film, but merely an isolated vignette. And so the film abruptly jumps to 1944, the story now focused on Shoshana Dreyfus (Melanie Laurent), owner of a small Paris cinema (inherited from her aunt and uncle), and pursued romantically by a German war hero, Frederick Zoller (Daniel Bruhl). The film then cuts to the second nicely constructed scene that takes place in a Parisian bistro, involving British and American soldiers dressed in Nazi uniforms, their mission being to contact German movie star Bridget von Hammersmark (Diane Kruger), a British undercover agent. Like the opening, this set piece is fraught with tension, is wonderfully shot, and even with its concluding Mexican standoff represents Tarantino at his best. But where the film falls away is in its inability to tell a fully coherent story with compelling characters that connect with each other and with the audience. Ultimately, despite the vignettes, or because of the disparate vignettes, there is no there there; the film has no sustaining center. Tarantino can almost blithely skirt the horror of the extermination of the Jews, perpetrated by monsters like Landa, and turn Landa, decked out in his tailored SS uniform and gleaming black riding boots, into the most attractive and authentic hustler in the film. This is not a film about distilled evil but about scenarios leading to a blazing climax where revisionist history takes place inside a burning cinema in Paris. If Schindler’s List is the yin, then Inglourious Basterds is the yang. Regarding the unusual spelling of the film’s title – Inglourious Basterds – apparently it’s an obscure reference to an Italian knock-off film of The Dirty Dozen, reflecting nothing more than Tarantino’s quirky style and no more. Inglourious Basterds. Starring Christop Waltz, Brad Pitt, Diane Kruger, and Melanie Laurent. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. 2 hrs., 32 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. articles.text: Whether it’s men in tights or Gladiator haute couture, the legend of Robin Hood is mythic, the stuff of high adventure. Hollywood has been enamored of this character for decades, always eager to give the tale a new twist, or give the actor du jour an opportunity to don costume and take up residence in Sherwood Forest. One incarnation of Robin Hood searches for originality with Ridley Scott (Alien, Blade Runner, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, and Kingdom of Heaven) directing and Brian Hegeland (L.A. Confidential) writing the script. Scott and Hegeland, deciding to add to the legend, set about answering the central backstory question: who was Robin before he was, well, Robin, prior to the time when he and he and his band of outlaws were ensconced in Sherwood Forest from whence they stole from the rich and gave to the poor (called wealth distribution today). Because Hollywood practices revisionist history with conviction and insouciance, the year, instead of 1185, is 1199. But who’s counting? Robin (Russell Crowe), we are told, is Robin Longstride, a commoner and master archer with the army of King Richard the Lionheart, who, after a decade-long crusade in the Holy Land, is on his way back to England. Crossing France, he lays siege to a well-defended castle. It is during that battle that the film opens and where we meet Longstride and what will eventually be his crew of Merry Men – Little John (Kevin Durand), Will Scarlett (Scott Grimes) and Allan A’Dayle (Alan Doyle). Longstride and his crew conclude, after King Richard is killed when a French castle cook drops a pot of stew and takes random aim with a crossbow, that they have served the crown long enough and decide to make their own way back to England. It is Russell Crowe stars in Ridley Scott’s Robin Hood on that trip that Robin’s future is changed forever. It’s tempting to recount what proves to be a convoluted tale. Suffice it to say that he lands in London under an alias, Robert of Loxley, and makes his way to Nottingham where he returns a sword to Sir Walter Loxley (Max von Sydow), father of Robert. He also meets Robert’s widow, Marion (Cate Blanchette). Chemistry is afoot. Thus far, the story of how Robin Longstride becomes Robert of Loxley/Robin of Loxley is appealing; however, it lacks a sharp edge. There is, eventually, palace intrigue, perpetrated by the newly crowned John, Richard’s brother. And there is the duplicitous Sir Godfrey (Mark Strong), newly anointed chancellor and tax collector, who prepares, surreptitiously, to betray England to France for power and fortune. Nevertheless, even with the signature battle scenes, for which director Scott is famous, the film is missing something at its center. Crowe, always a bit distant and laconic, now all but middle-aged and beefy, never conveys jeopardy or urgency as he did in Master and Commander and L.A. Confidential. Even with the epic battle on the English shore, fending off a French army prepared to invade England once again, there is an absence of the tension that Scott is so brilliant at creating, examples being Gladiator and Black Hawk Down. That isn’t to say that Robin Hood lacks a certain intensity. It is, after all, a Ridley Scott film, one brought to life by some of the finest actors working today. And keep in mind that as this story ends, King John declares Robin an outlaw prompting Robin to retreat to Sherwood Forest where he will take up his bow and his sword against King John and cohorts. Robin Hood. Directed by Ridley Scott. Starring Russell Crowe, Cate Blanchette, Mark Strong, Oscar Isaac. and Max von Sydow. 2 hrs., 19 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime.

articles.text: Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E, Up will delight and entertain audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail. Written and directed by Piedmont resident Pete Docter, it won an Academy Award, among many awards. It is breathtaking, and the story is a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. All that is absent from this touching retrospective is that one, magnificent adventure. Sadly, having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, wellequipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell, Carl’s being that poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Directed by Pete Docter. Animated with the voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. A scene from Pixar Animations’ UP.

First of all, Willamette Valley is huge. Its 150-mile length runs from just south of Portland all the way to Eugene. Today it is synonymous with “Oregon Wine Country” and contains more than 19,000 acres of vineyards and over 500 wineries. Several things struck me as I toured the region for the first time. First was its overall beauty. Compared to California everything was so green. The rolling hills were lush with evergreen and deciduous trees and the vineyards were perfectly manicured. Second, there was a relaxed vibe that reminded me I was far from Napa Valley where wine tasting now seems to be a contact sport. We never encountered a winery that was overcrowded with tourists and the roads were free of traffic. Third. my friend Kent who has spent his life in the wine business, remarked on the professionalism and extreme hospitality of every wine industry worker we met. articles.text: one of 20 cemeteries in Paris, and the largest and best known. Composer Fréderic Chopin, writers Honoré de Balzac, Marcel Proust, Oscar Wilde, and Gertrude Stein, banker James Rothschild, jeweler René Lalique; singer Edith Piaf, rock star Jim Morrison, painters Amadeo Modigliani, Camille Pissarro, Eugène Delacroix; actresses Simone Signoret and Sarah Bernhardt, and mime Marcel Marceau are buried here. Several sections are devoted to wartime heroes and victims with achingly stark, but beautiful monuments to memorialize those who lost their lives at Nazi extermination and concentration camps. Father Francois de la Chaise The Jesuits had settled originally on this hillside in the 1620s and built a retreat for aging priests. When later converted to a cemetery, it was named after Father François de la Chaise, confessor to Louis XIV and patron of the Jesuits. Under Napoleon the tract of land was bought in 1804 by the City of Paris to expand graveyards beyond the city, because inner-city cemeteries were overflowing, plus taking up valuable real estate. Parisians didn’t warm to the plan for relocating their loved ones’ graves to the outer reaches of the city; and Roman Catholics resisted burials on unconsecrated land. To spur business, the government with great fanfare relocated the graves of popular figures such as Molière, France’s greatest playwright, and poet-fabulist Jean de La Fontaine. The burial business grew. Heloise and Abelard To further promote burials in the countryside graveyard, the remains of Pierre Abélard and Héloise d’Argenteuil (d’ar-gentway) were transported to the new site. The 12th Century Héloise and Abélard were among the most famous star-crossed lovers in French history. For nearly nine hundred years, the legendary romance has been studied through their eight surviving love letters. Héloise was the daughter born of an illicit affair between her mother, likely a nun, and her lover. She grew to be a beautiful, gifted young woman under the tutelage of her uncle Fulbert, a high placed church canon (i.e., board of directors). Her uncle raised Héloise, and he educated her well in the classics, languages, and the arts. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, August 9, 2023 AMERICANS IN PARIS By P K Forsyth The most visited necropolis in the world is Père Lachaise cemetery. This is a bucolic place, perched under several thousand trees, where the air is cooler than the tangent city streets of the 20th arrondissement toward the east. The cemetery slopes gently on a hillside, while some terrain is rocky, and sidewalks wander off into pathways. Resting stones give way over time and into a slapdash array, especially, it seems, when one is in search of a famous gravesite. There are hundreds of famous gravesites, and so, expect a hike – and a search. Père Lachaise is The gravesite monument of Héloise and Abélard as they lie together in eternity. Whether their remains exist at this site, is disputed. Héloise and Abélard, as they may have appeared when they fell in love during the 12th C. in Paris. A visit to Pere LaChaise Cimetaire one of 20 cemeteries in Paris, and the largest and best known. Composer Fréderic Chopin, writers Honoré de Balzac, Marcel Proust, Oscar Wilde, and Gertrude Stein, banker James Rothschild, jeweler René Lalique; singer Edith Piaf, rock star Jim Morrison, painters Amadeo Modigliani, Camille Pissarro, Eugène Delacroix; actresses Simone Signoret and Sarah Bernhardt, and mime Marcel Marceau are buried here. Several sections are devoted to wartime heroes and victims with achingly stark, but beautiful monuments to memorialize those who lost their lives at Nazi extermination and concentration camps. Father Francois de la Chaise The Jesuits had settled originally on this hillside in the 1620s and built a retreat for aging priests. When later converted to a cemetery, it was named after Father François de la Chaise, confessor to Louis XIV and patron of the Jesuits. Under Napoleon the tract of land was bought in 1804 by the City of Paris to expand graveyards beyond the city, because inner-city cemeteries were overflowing, plus taking up valuable real estate. Parisians didn’t warm to the plan for relocating their loved ones’ graves to the outer reaches of the city; and Roman Catholics resisted burials on unconsecrated land. To spur business, the government with great fanfare relocated the graves of popular figures such as Molière, France’s greatest playwright, and poet-fabulist Jean de La Fontaine. The burial business grew. Heloise and Abelard To further promote burials in the countryside graveyard, the remains of Pierre Abélard and Héloise d’Argenteuil (d’ar-gentway) were transported to the new site. The 12th Century Héloise and Abélard were among the most famous star-crossed lovers in French history. For nearly nine hundred years, the legendary romance has been studied through their eight surviving love letters. Héloise was the daughter born of an illicit affair between her mother, likely a nun, and her lover. She grew to be a beautiful, gifted young woman under the tutelage of her uncle Fulbert, a high placed church canon (i.e., board of directors). Her uncle raised Héloise, and he educated her well in the classics, languages, and the arts. She was already known academically for her insightful writings from the feminine viewpoint when she arrived in Paris and met Pierre Abélard who would become her tutor. Abélard was born into minor nobility and from a young age showed genius at scholarly learning. He eschewed the traditional military career and knighthood of his father and chose philosophy and the life of a theologian The beloved chanteuse Edith Piaf is in the same burial plot as her only child who tragically died at age two. Fresh mementos are placed on her grave. The crematorium was built in 1890s after French law authorized cremations, but it remained uncommon until the Catholic church overturned the cremation ban in 1963. Today, cremation represents 45% of burials in Paris. A French soldier’s gravestone: Memory of Regret, “our 17-year-old assassinated by the Nazis.” at the cathedral school of Notre Dame of Paris. His rose in popularity, drawing thousands of students. His attraction to Héloise, he later wrote in a letter, caused his teaching career to go awry. Despite his dedication to theology and vow of celibacy, Abélard struck an arrangement with Fulbert to tutor Héloise in exchange for boarding at Fulbert’s house and pursued the affair. Abélard may have boasted of the affair and his conquest. Fulbert was angered and separated the pair, but they continued to meet secretly. When Héloise became pregnant, Abélard sent her to his family’s home in Brittany to be cared for, and she bore a son. Fulbert pressed them to marry, but Abélard resisted, concerned that his career path could be in jeopardy, unless the marriage was kept secret. She opposed the idea of a secret marriage or any marriage, but gave in, and they did marry. Abélard whisked her away to Argenteuil convent to keep her safe from her uncle’s anger. Fulbert, convinced that Abélard was casting Héloise aside, and enraged about the downfall of his own reputation, sent a band of men into Abélard’s room in the dead of night and castrated Abélard. Humiliated and shamed, Abélard fled Paris and teaching to join a monastery. Héloise eventually rose to abbess at the Oratory of the Paraclete, a Benedictine monastery founded by Peter Abélard. The lovers continue to be a popular topic of inquiry today. Although the reburial of their remains at Père Lachaise contributed to the extraordinary success of the cemetery, their remains’ precise location is in dispute. See Americans in Paris on page 25

articles.text: Another strong summer showing of 39 walkers and five K-9 best friends was on hand for the Walking on Wednesdays group last week, August 2. Each year the group tries to walk every safe walking street in Piedmont. When they visit streets that border Oakland, there is an opportunity to see some great Oakland streets, too. A Piedmont street very few people ever go to is Florada Avenue on the southern border of Piedmont. At the end of Florada, just beyond the Oakland/Piedmont city line, is an impressive cactus garden in the front yard of an Oakland home. The walkers went on Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and then to Wildwood Gardens. They recalled that this was the entrance to Frank C. Havens’ “Wildwood” estate in the early 1900s. They appreciated the redwood tree just beyond the old pillars that once marked the entrance to Wildwood. The tree seems to have been fed for decades by underground water that has led to its huge size. In Wildwood Gardens the walkers noted a home built on stilts above the ravine below, another home with a long swing in its front yard, and a sizable tree house in the backyard of a home. When the group came to the end of Wildwood Gardens they passed by the seldom visited Wistaria Way, and emerged on Woodland Way. At its end the walkers were at a street that to the left is Lafayette Avenue and to the right is La Salle Avenue. There is no clear explanation why. It’s one of the street naming mysteries in Piedmont and Oakland. The group came to the little traveled Florada Avenue and went directly to Dick and Mary Carter’s home. Dick didn’t have refreshments ready for the walkers so they pressed on down the street to the Oakland boarder, where for yet another unknown reason the street becomes Portal Avenue. On Portal they came to a beautiful cactus garden in a front yard. Some walkers remembered talking with the homeowner on a past walk a few years before. The garden is now full, complete, and lovely. The walkers took a group photo in front of it. Farther down the street was a large, colorful, pink bougainvillea, however tree stumps along the hillside indicated some past tree falling issues. The walkers came to Ashmount Avenue which required an uphill climb. They were impressed by the lovely, large homes, many of which were built during the 1920s when Piedmont also experienced a building boom. Some walkers remembered that in the past the group had been able to visit and shop a farmer’s market that operated by a young entrepreneur out of the garage of his parents’ home on Ashmount. But he has moved and there was no produce for the walkers to take home. However, the walkers noticed a distinguished house designed by Bernard Maybeck, a UC Berkeley architecture professor and Julia Morgan’s teacher in the late nineteenth century. Maybeck also designed the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco. With all the walking, sightseeing, and talking, the morning was getting on and it was time to return by way of Mandana Avenue, which also changes its name to Crocker Avenue upon entering Piedmont from Oakland. The group took a direct route back to the Community Hall parking lot. It had been about a three mile walk with interesting homes, stories, and street name mysteries. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Thirty-nine walkers and five K-9 friends participated in last Wednesday’s walk. But there’s one important action that’s sometimes overlooked by retirees: sharing their financial situation with their grown children. And this knowledge can benefit everyone in your family. You might be surprised by the concern your children have for your financial well-being. Consider these findings from a 2023 study by Age Wave and Edward Jones: • 66% of millennials (generally defined as ranging from 27 to 42) worry that their parents or in-laws may not have enough money to live comfortably in retirement. • 83% of millennials would rather know their parents are financially secure in their retirement, even if it means their parents pass on less money to them. If you have children in this age range or older, or who soon will be, how can you address their concerns and potentially improve your financial outlook? Communication is the key. By openly communicating with your family about your financial status, you can reduce anxieties and misperceptions. If you’re in good financial shape, your adult children may be reassured that you won’t be needing their assistance. And if you are feeling some financial pressures, you can inform your children of the steps you are taking to improve your situation. One such step may be to reduce your cost of living — the less you spend day to day, the better your ability to preserve your investment and retirement accounts. You may be able to reduce costs in many small ways, such as ending streaming services you no longer use, but you could make an even bigger impact by downsizing your living arrangements. In fact, 72% of today’s retirees have downsized or are willing to downsize to reduce their housing costs, according to the Age Wave/Edward Jones survey. Downsizing isn’t for everyone, but if it’s a possibility for you, it may be worth considering because the savings could be significant. You may also be able to reduce or consolidate your debts. Start by understanding how much and what kinds of debt you have. Then, consider ways to lower your payments, such as refinancing. For example, if you’re carrying a balance on multiple credit cards, you might be able to transfer the amounts you owe onto a single card with a more favorable interest rate. Here’s another move to consider: Adjust your investment mix to possibly provide you with more income in retirement. During your working years, you may have invested primarily for growth — after all, you could be retired for two or more decades, so you’ll need to draw on as many financial assets as possible. But once you’re retired, your investment focus may need to shift somewhat toward income-producing opportunities. Keep in mind, though, that you’ll still need some growth potential to help keep ahead of inflation. One final suggestion: Let your children know if you already have a strategy in place to meet the potentially high costs of longterm care, such as a nursing home stay. This burden is certainly something you won’t want your children to take on. By informing your children about your financial picture, and how you’re trying to improve it, you can ease everyone’s minds — so keep the lines of communication open. articles.text: your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. The Pilgrim’s Path goes for 0.8 of a mile until greeting the road, once again, where you will follow the road up for the remaining half-mile up to Doi Suthep, where you will pass shops, restaurants, and taxi drivers at the bottom of the temple. Created in 1383, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is named after the mountain which it is located and considered to be the most sacred temple in all of Thailand. There’s another magnificent Naga Staircase leading to the temple, this one much larger and colorful than the previous at Wat Pha Lat. Peer closely at the scales of the two serpents leading you towards Doi Suthep. Entrance to the monastery costs ฿100, which is just $2.85— it is also recommended to dress appropriately. You’ll find sweeping views of Chiang Mai from multiple overlooks on the grounds and several large statues of Buddha. You’ll also be required to take your shoes off when entering the primary section of the temple, where there’s a spectacular large golden Chedi, which towers 79 feet in height. Should hikers call it a day, you’ll end your hike at around 2.5 miles with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain. Taxis will be ready at the base of Doi Suthep to take your group back into town. Heading back down the road and onto the trails makes it a 4.5 mile day of hiking. Keep in mind some steep sections coupled with usual wet conditions in Thailand could make things difficult for a descent. Hikers should wear proper footgear for tackling the Monk’s Trail and Pilgrim’s Trail, along with packing mosquito repellent to keep away the pesky critters. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, August 9, 2023 Gran Torino Continued from page 20 principled and courageous. When a family of Hmongs – people from the hills of Thailand, Laos and Vietnam – move in nextdoor, Kowalski regards them as “slopes” and “zipper heads.” His prejudice is undisguised and blunt. He survived Korea, won the Silver Star, and has little desire to get to know these people he views as unwelcome and unfamiliar. At least until events make it impossible for him to remain apart and then he involves himself in a world that surprises him. Slowly, he becomes a neighbor. Gran Torino is eminently entertaining, if for no other reason to observe the changes Kowalski goes through as he takes a Hmong boy, Thao (Bee Vang) under his old man’s wing and becomes his protector. It’s impossible, with this film especially, to watch Eastwood on screen and separate him from the character Kowalski, in the same way that Cruise, no matter the role, is always Cruise. For an actor, it’s a strength and it’s a weakness. While these actors can inhabit a part, they can never completely submerge themselves to the point that the audience forgets who they are. We’re watching Eastwood doing Harry, doing Kowalski. In one scene, Kowalski points a vintage M-16 rifle at a gang member and snarls, through clenched teeth, “Get off of my lawn.” Ah, yes. You feeling lucky, punk? Are you? Is Gran Torino worth an afternoon and the price of a ticket? Definitely. It’s a familiar but involving story, and all the performances are excellent. There are moments of high tension and other moments that are downright comical and will make you laugh. Gran Torino. Starring Clint Eastwood, Christopher Carley, Bee Vang and Ashley Her.
